notes: ROUND 2. Both round-1 majors are genuinely fixed and I could not break either fix in the way it was broken before. F1: measured -- pod\"1, pod\\1, pod\u0001, pod\n and the field-injection endpoint are all refused at construction; every legal value I tried round-trips byte-exact (empty endpoint, whitespace-only endpoint, trailing space, '-' and '/', non-BMP surrogate PAIRS, DEL 0x7F, NEL 0x85, U+2028, U+2029, Long.MAX_VALUE in both numeric fields). Refusing at construction rather than escaping is the right call and the right moment: escaping added after M4.3b/M5 have written leases changes the bytes of an existing shape and is a format change under non-negotiable 8, whereas narrowing the domain before the first lease exists costs nothing. rejectUnrepresentable runs after the podId blank check and before the expiry check, and its message carries only the field name, the index and the hex code point -- never the value -- so security.md rule 4 holds. F2: I could not fool the canonical comparison. Because every accepted input must equal encode(parsed) byte for byte, any mis-parse is self-detecting; it also closes a laxness I found in longField, where Character.isDigit plus Long.parseLong accept Arabic-Indic digits (measured: epoch U+0663 parses as 3 and is then refused as non-canonical). decode(encode(x)) == x still holds for every legal value listed above. Strict canonical form is the right call and no leniency is needed: leading and trailing whitespace is ALREADY tolerated via strip() (measured -- a lease written with echo and a trailing newline decodes), which covers the cat/operator case; only internal pretty-printing is refused, and the write path is code, never a human. The IllegalArgumentException|NullPointerException catch is complete for reachable unchecked exceptions -- I traced every charAt and substring in decode/stringField/longField and no IndexOutOfBoundsException is reachable (the shape guard gives length >= 2, both helpers return before any negative-range substring) -- and it loses nothing, since the cause is chained and the input is in the message. F3: the checkpoint-pointer prohibition is present in M4.3b's row and correctly worded. Test-review carry-overs verified from the production side: the shape guard (length < 2, first char, last char) is correct and truncate-by-one now lands on it; the missing-string-field guard is correct and {} exits through the epoch lookup first, as the test comment says. NOTHING PRE-EMPTS M4.8: the record carries no checkpoint pointer, and decode actively refuses one. But M4.8 needs to know the consequence this diff creates -- with no version field and unknown fields refused outright, any future lease field is a flag day: an un-upgraded pod's decode throws IOException and, in this class's own words, 'leadership would be undecidable'. That belongs in M4.8's mandated ADR. COST: none -- pure encode/decode in format, no store access, no LIST, no per-record/shard/index request; decode's extra encode() is CPU on a path that runs about 0.33 times a second per pod. M4.3b CAN be built on this without inventing a decision: no TTL, no key grammar, no clock, no store; epoch 0 is documented as the first valid epoch. Deliberately NOT re-run: the suite and check-module, which the packet lists as passed gates. F4 is the finding I came closest to raising as major; I did not, because rule 12's remedy for a round-2 blocker is to SPLIT the commit, and the fix here is one line in a file the split already conceptually touches -- so 'too big' would be a false diagnosis. It should be fixed when M4.3b lands.

findings.summary: The M4.3/M4.3b split was written into backlog.md but not into the SPEC's task table, which still assigns acquire/renew/release, the key grammar, the putIfAbsent/putIfMatch pair and TTL-as-configuration to M4.3 -- the row this commit marks done -- and has no M4.3b row at all. sdd.md rule 8: a spec that turns out to be wrong is amended, not worked around.
findings.failure_scenario: SPEC.md:505 reads 'M4.3 | Lease record and key grammar; acquire/renew/release -- putIfAbsent for FIRST acquisition ... TTL and renew interval as configuration', while backlog.md:113 now scopes M4.3 to the record alone and marks it done. Anyone checking M4 for completeness against the SPEC's own task table -- which is what M4.15 (VERIFIED.md and the milestone review) does, and what the milestone-review skill reads -- sees M4.3 done and concludes the two acquisition paths and the TTL rule shipped, when neither exists in the tree. This is the exact failure mode the M4.0 row records as recurring across four rounds: 'fixing ONE copy of a fact and missing its duplicates in the tables that decide what gets built'. The repo's own precedent shows the SPEC table is meant to carry split rows -- M1/SPEC.md's task table lists M1.3b, M1.16b, M1.16c, M1.17b and M1.19b beside their parents. Fix in the M4.3b commit: narrow SPEC.md:505 to the record and add an M4.3b row carrying the orchestration clauses.

findings.summary: The class javadoc still carries the unsound defence round 1 flagged. Lines 31-34 justify 'no escaping' with 'a podId refuses - and / upstream and an endpoint is host:port', and the constructor comment 35 lines below refutes it by name. The record is now correct; its primary documentation still states the wrong reason.
findings.failure_scenario: Measured against the staged code: new Lease(1, "a-b/c", "e", 5L) is ACCEPTED, so 'a podId refuses - and /' is not true of this record even as a description of its values -- and the constructor comment at :67-69 says outright that the guard 'lives in another module and would not have refused a quote'. The file therefore asserts both the claim and its refutation. Concrete cost: at M5 the endpoint becomes non-empty and someone may add a fifth string field (a peer address, a zone). A reader who takes the class javadoc at face value concludes that upstream validation is what makes escaping unnecessary, adds the field to encode() and does not add it to rejectUnrepresentable -- reopening F1 exactly, with the same silent field-injection decode. Delete the em-dash clause; the true reason (the constructor refuses what the encoder cannot represent) is already written 35 lines down.

findings.summary: The refusal is not complete: an UNPAIRED SURROGATE passes rejectUnrepresentable (it is neither quote, backslash, nor < 0x20) and is then silently replaced by '?' by String.getBytes(UTF_8), so the round trip changes the holder identity with no exception -- and the canonical comparison cannot see it, because both sides of the comparison are derived after the loss.
findings.failure_scenario: MEASURED against the staged code, compiled standalone. new Lease(1, "x\uD800", "e", 5L) is accepted; encode() emits bytes 78 3F; decode() returns holderPodId="x?" and throws nothing -- decode(encode(x)) != x, silently, which is the precise wording of the round-1 F1 defect. Worse in kind: Arrays.equals(new Lease(1,"x\uD800",...).encode(), new Lease(1,"x\uDC00",...).encode()) is TRUE, so two distinct podIds serialise to the same lease and cannot be told apart by a reader. The related case: invalid UTF-8 in the stored bytes is normalised to U+FFFD by `new String(bytes, UTF_8)` and accepted as canonical (measured: a lone 0xC3 in the podId decodes to [70 fffd 64] with no error), so decode cannot detect a corrupted holder. Both are UNREACHABLE from the real value sources -- a Kubernetes POD_NAME and a host:port are ASCII -- which is why this is minor and not a repeat major. One line closes it: reject when Character.isSurrogate(c) (or assert !s.equals(new String(s.getBytes(UTF_8), UTF_8)) once), alongside the existing three tests in aHolderFieldContainingJsonHostileCharactersIsRefused.
findings.verifies: F1 -- fix incomplete at the edge

findings.summary: decode's operator-facing messages misdiagnose the one case an operator actually creates. A hand-edited, pretty-printed lease fails with 'lease has a non-numeric epoch' about an epoch that plainly is a number, and 'lease is not in canonical form' never says what the canonical form is.
findings.failure_scenario: MEASURED: Lease.decode of {"epoch": 1, "holderPodId": "p", "holderEndpoint": "", "expiresAtMillis": 5} throws IOException 'lease has a non-numeric epoch: {"epoch": 1, ...}'. The real cause is the space after the colon; longField starts scanning at the space, finds no digit, and reports the value type. An operator repairing a lease during an outage -- the exact audience the hand-rolled JSON codec is justified by, and the reason this file is .json at all -- reads that its epoch is not a number, sees the number, and has no path forward. Same for the canonical-form message, which withholds the one string that would fix the file. Neither is a correctness defect and neither is worth another round; cheapest fix when M4.3b lands is to have decode append the expected canonical encoding to both messages (parsed.encode() is already in hand at :167) and to have longField say 'expected a bare integer immediately after "<name>":'.

findings.summary: The M4.3 row's completeness claim is stale: 'All 11 mutation verified' against a test file that now holds 17 @Test methods. Both numbers cannot be right, and the row is marked done.
findings.failure_scenario: grep -c '@Test' format/src/test/java/binjava/format/LeaseTest.java returns 17; the row claims 11. Either six tests were added in the round-1 fix without being mutation-verified -- which the row does not say -- or the count is left over from round 1. A later reader auditing which tests earned a red (M4.15, or anyone re-opening the codec) takes the row as the record of what was verified and has no way to tell which six are unaccounted for. Non-negotiable 4 makes numbers in a done row load-bearing. The sentence is also missing a word ('All 11 mutation verified'), which is how the staleness escaped notice.
